title: The old cook
hookLine: the young Dogen meets an old monastery cook drying mushrooms in the sun who won't let anyone else do it

cards: Mushrooms, spread out to dry on a stone walkway at a Chinese monastery. The midday sun is fierce, and the stone is hot enough to feel through sandals. Out on it, bent over them, is the monastery's cook.

He is old, his eyebrows white, no hat, a bamboo staff in his hand, sweat running down his face. A young Japanese monk, visiting to study, stops and stares. Why is this old man doing this, now, himself?
The young monk was Dogen, and he wrote the scene down years later. Today, tenzo.

teach.b: First, the job. The cook in a Zen monastery, the tenzo, was not a kitchen hand. It was a senior post, held by an experienced monk, because feeding the community was treated as practice of the highest seriousness.
Dogen wrote a whole work about it, Instructions for the Cook, and this meeting is at its heart. Second, the question. Dogen asked the old man why he didn't have a helper or a worker do it.
The cook answered, in Dogen's telling: others are not me. Your line comes from that. Not someone else.
Third, the follow-up. Dogen pressed: fine, but why now, in the worst of the heat?
The cook said: if not now, when? Dogen had no reply. He wrote that only then did he begin to understand what the cook's work really was.
Fourth, what it means. The cook isn't refusing help out of pride. His practice is his own, and it happens in this hour, with these mushrooms.
Handing it off, or putting it off until a better time, would be handing off his own life.
For Dogen, who had come all the way to China looking for the teaching in scriptures and great halls, it was a surprise to find it on a hot walkway, in an old man's sweat.
In this telling, the kitchen, the sink, even the inbox, are not interruptions to practice.

teach.h: NO ONE ELSE CAN DO YOURS.
teach.b: They are the practice, and no one else can do yours.

how: In Soto Zen monasteries, Dogen's Instructions for the Cook guides the kitchen, and the tenzo prepares meals as a form of practice, with care for each ingredient and the people who will eat.

games.q: you're the old cook, sweating in the midday sun over the mushrooms. a young monk asks why you don't let a helper do it. what do you say?
o: there's no one free to help
games.why: the cook said: others are not me. and when Dogen asked why now, in the heat: if not now, when?

practice: Bring to mind one task you've been hoping someone else will handle, or keep moving to later: a call, a dish, a form, an apology.
Picture yourself doing it plainly, hear out any reasons that rise for not now, and set them on the counter. Then quietly ask yourself the cook's question: if not now, when?

wordCard.voice: Tenzo. The senior monastery cook's post, held by the old man who told young Dogen: others are not me, and if not now, when? Today's word.

orig.note: Japanese tenzo: the monastery cook, a senior post in a Zen community.

carryVoice: Your line: not someone else. His practice happened in this hour, with these mushrooms. See you tomorrow.
